WhatItMeans: People take it to mean that no season lasts forever: hard times will end, and good times will too, so hold steady and do not cling too tightly to either.
WhatTheBibleSays: Scripture agrees that seasons change: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven" (Ecclesiastes 3:1), and Paul calls present affliction "but for a moment" beside eternal glory (2 Corinthians 4:17). But the Bible does not stop at impermanence: it anchors hope in what does not pass, God's word and His promises, which endure when everything else fades. My position is that the saying is true as far as it goes, but on its own it is only half a comfort; the full comfort is that the God who outlasts every season is holding us through it.
Origin: A Persian fable about a king who asks his wise men for a sentence true in every circumstance and receives a ring engraved with these words, told in the poetry of the 12th-century Sufi poets Sanai and Attar of Nishapur. It reached English through Edward FitzGerald's retelling in 1852 and Abraham Lincoln's speech at Milwaukee on 30 September 1859.
Sources: Attar of Nishapur, Ilahi-Nama (12th century); Edward FitzGerald, Polonius (1852); Abraham Lincoln, Address to the Wisconsin State Agricultural Society (30 September 1859); on-site KJV text
